title: Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena
authors: Lianmin Zheng, Wei-Lin Chiang, Ying Sheng, et al.
key_findings: Position bias (default pairwise prompt, answers swapped): consistency Claude-v1 23.8% (75% biased to first), GPT-3.5 46.2%, GPT-4 65.0% (30% biased to first)
Verbosity 'repetitive list' attack failure rate: Claude-v1 91.3%, GPT-3.5 91.3%, GPT-4 8.7%
Self-enhancement: GPT-4 favoured itself ~10 points and Claude-v1 ~25 points above human estimate, but authors say data too limited to conclude
Math grading failures: default 70%, chain-of-thought 30%, reference-guided 15%
Few-shot examples raised GPT-4 position consistency 65.0% -> 77.5%
GPT-4 pairwise agreement with humans 85% on non-tie votes vs human-human 81%; humans found GPT-4's disagreeing verdicts reasonable in 75% of cases
practical_applications: Always judge pairs in both orders; count a win only if it survives the swap
Give the AI critic a reference (brief, real product photo, script) — reference-guided grading cut errors most
Watch for length/verbosity: longer critique or longer caption is not better
limitations: Text chat answers, 2023 models; numbers will differ for current and multimodal models
Self-enhancement evidence inconclusive by the authors' own account

title: Large Language Models are not Fair Evaluators
authors: Peiyi Wang, Lei Li, Liang Chen, et al.
key_findings: Ranking of candidate responses can be hacked by changing order: Vicuna-13B beat ChatGPT on 66/80 queries with ChatGPT as judge

Mitigations: Multiple Evidence Calibration (explain before scoring, several chains), Balanced Position Calibration (score both orders and aggregate), Human-in-the-Loop Calibration (entropy flags hard items for a human)
practical_applications: Critic writes located evidence before the score
Flag A/B pairs where the verdict flips with order for human review
limitations: Text-only, ChatGPT/GPT-4 era

title: LLM Evaluators Recognize and Favor Their Own Generations
authors: Arjun Panickssery, Samuel R. Bowman, Shi Feng
key_findings: GPT-4, GPT-3.5 and Llama 2 prefer their own summaries over other LLMs' and humans' (pairwise GPT-4 self-preference 0.705 XSUM, 0.912 CNN/DM)
Models recognise their own text above chance; GPT-4 73.5% vs two LLMs + humans
Self-recognition and self-preference correlate linearly across fine-tuning runs; swapping source labels reversed GPT-4's preference
Authors suggest authorship obfuscation as a possible standard practice (not tested)
practical_applications: Do not let the model that generated a prompt/caption be the only judge; hide which version came from whom
Use a different model or a human for final selection
limitations: Summarisation only; quality not controlled against ground truth so some preference may be justified; causal claim not mechanistically validated

title: A Survey on LLM-as-a-Judge
authors: Jiawei Gu, Xuhui Jiang, et al.
key_findings: Frames the core question as how to build reliable LLM judges: improve consistency, mitigate biases, adapt to scenarios
Proposes meta-evaluation benchmark; notes trade-offs such as robustness vs sensitivity
practical_applications: Treat the AI critic's reliability as something to measure, not assume
limitations: Preprint survey, revised many times; read abstract only

title: MLLM-as-a-Judge: Assessing Multimodal LLM-as-a-Judge with Vision-Language Benchmark
authors: Dongping Chen, Ruoxi Chen, Shilin Zhang, et al.
key_findings: Multimodal LLMs are human-like in Pair Comparison but diverge significantly from humans in Scoring Evaluation and Batch Ranking
Persistent biases (egocentric, position, length), hallucinated judgments and inconsistency even in GPT-4V
practical_applications: For images, prefer pairwise A-vs-B questions over absolute 0-10 scores from an AI critic
Ask the critic to point to the location of each issue so hallucinated issues can be checked
limitations: 2024 models; image-text tasks not specifically aesthetic/creative

title: AesBench: An Expert Benchmark for Multimodal Large Language Models on Image Aesthetics Perception
authors: Yipo Huang, et al.
key_findings: Expert-labelled aesthetics database; four abilities: perception, empathy, assessment, interpretation
15 MLLMs incl. GPT-4V and Gemini Pro Vision show only rudimentary aesthetic perception, significant gap to humans
practical_applications: AI aesthetic verdicts (taste layer P) deserve the least trust; AI checks of technical layer T are more defensible
limitations: Preprint; early-2024 models; newer models untested here

title: Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
authors: Jie Huang, Xinyun Chen, Swaroop Mishra, et al.
key_findings: Without oracle labels, intrinsic self-correction lowered accuracy: GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 -> 38.1; GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 -> 89.0
Models changed correct answers to wrong more often than the reverse — 'cannot properly judge the correctness of their reasoning'
Earlier gains relied on oracle labels; multi-agent debate did not beat self-consistency at equal sample count
Self-correction helps with external feedback (tests, tools, verifiers)
practical_applications: A 'please review your own work' pass by the same model is not an independent critique; give it external evidence (measurements, reference photo, script diff)
Do not ask the critic to 'find problems' when none are needed — it may change what was right
limitations: Reasoning tasks, not aesthetic tasks; tone/safety rewrites may behave differently

title: When Can LLMs Actually Correct Their Own Mistakes? A Critical Survey of Self-Correction of LLMs
authors: Ryo Kamoi, Yusen Zhang, Nan Zhang, Jiawei Han, Rui Zhang
key_findings: No prior work shows successful self-correction with feedback from prompted LLMs except in tasks exceptionally suited to it
Self-correction works well when reliable external feedback exists; large-scale fine-tuning enables it
Many studies over-evaluate self-correction through vague questions or unfair comparisons
practical_applications: Build the critic loop around external checks (tools, reference images, human), not self-reflection alone
limitations: Fast-moving field; survey of LLM text tasks

title: G-Eval: NLG Evaluation using GPT-4 with Better Human Alignment
authors: Yang Liu, Dan Iter, Yichong Xu, Shuohang Wang, Ruochen Xu, Chenguang Zhu
key_findings: Chain-of-thought evaluation steps + form-filling; GPT-4 Spearman 0.514 with humans on summarisation
Flags potential bias of LLM evaluators towards LLM-generated texts (self-reinforcement risk if used as reward)
practical_applications: Let the critic derive explicit evaluation steps from the brief before scoring
limitations: Moderate correlation only; summarisation and dialogue

title: Humans or LLMs as the Judge? A Study on Judgement Bias
authors: Guiming Hardy Chen, Shunian Chen, Ziche Liu, Feng Jiang, Benyou Wang
key_findings: Tests misinformation-oversight, gender, authority and beauty biases in both human and LLM judges without ground truth
Both humans and LLM judges are vulnerable to perturbations; even cutting-edge judges have considerable biases; biases can be exploited to attack LLM judges
practical_applications: Polished formatting, citations or 'expert' framing can raise a score without raising quality — strip them before judging
limitations: Text QA; bias names differ between versions

title: Justice or Prejudice? Quantifying Biases in LLM-as-a-Judge
authors: Jiayi Ye, Yanbo Wang, Yue Huang, et al.
key_findings: CALM framework quantifies 12 bias types by principle-guided perturbation (e.g., position, verbosity, self-enhancement, authority, sentiment, refinement-aware)
Advanced models perform well overall but significant biases persist in specific tasks
practical_applications: Perturbation test for our own critic: change only order/label/length and see if the verdict moves
limitations: Full list of 12 biases taken from secondary summaries, abstract read only

title: Large Language Models are Inconsistent and Biased Evaluators
authors: Rickard Stureborg, Dimitris Alikaniotis, Yoshi Suhara
key_findings: LLM evaluators show familiarity bias (prefer low-perplexity text), skewed rating distributions, anchoring when several attributes are scored in one output
Low inter-sample agreement and sensitivity to prompt changes irrelevant to quality
practical_applications: Score each criterion in a separate call or at least before seeing a total; expect ratings to bunch — use pairwise or anchored scales
limitations: Preprint; SummEval/RoSE text summarisation

title: The effects of feedback interventions on performance: A historical review, a meta-analysis, and a preliminary feedback intervention theory
authors: Avraham N. Kluger, Angelo DeNisi
key_findings: 607 effect sizes, 23,663 observations: mean d = .41 but more than one third of feedback interventions decreased performance
Not explained by sampling error or feedback sign; FIT: effectiveness falls as feedback moves attention from the task towards the self
Moderators reported (via Hattie & Timperley 2007 Table 3): discouraging feedback -0.14, praise about the task 0.09, high threat to self-esteem 0.08, feedback on change from previous trials 0.55
practical_applications: Critique the work and the next action, never the maker
Show change vs the previous version
limitations: Mostly non-classroom lab/work tasks pre-1996; moderator numbers here are second-hand via Hattie & Timperley

title: The Power of Feedback
authors: John Hattie, Helen Timperley
key_findings: Feedback average effect 0.79 across syntheses but highly variable; cues 1.10, corrective 0.37, praise 0.14, programmed instruction -0.04
Three questions: Where am I going? How am I going? Where to next?
Four levels: task (FT), process (FP), self-regulation (FR), self (FS); FS least effective, FP and FR powerful
FT more powerful for faulty interpretations than for missing knowledge; too-specific FT can pull attention below the level needed
Timing: immediate helps task-level acquisition; delay helps on difficult/process items (Clariana et al.: delayed -0.06 easy, 1.17 difficult)
practical_applications: Every critique item states goal, gap and next step
Move from 'this pixel is wrong' to 'the process that causes it' when the same error repeats
limitations: Synthesis of classroom meta-analyses; Hattie's effect-size aggregation methods are criticised elsewhere (not reviewed here)

title: Feedback specificity, exploration, and learning
authors: Jodi S. Goodman, Robert E. Wood, Margaretha Hendrickx
key_findings: More specific feedback improved practice performance but the benefit did not last or transfer when the task changed
Specificity reduced exploration during practice; specific feedback helps early performance but can undermine learning for later independent performance
practical_applications: For a one-off deliverable be very specific; for building the maker's (or pipeline's) skill, add the principle, not only the pixel fix
limitations: Lab task; abstract-level reading via index

title: Almost an Expert: The Effects of Rubrics and Expertise on Perceived Value of Crowdsourced Design Critiques
authors: Alvin Yuan, Kurt Luther, Markus Krause, Sophie Isabel Vennix, Steven P. Dow, Björn Hartmann
key_findings: With an expert rubric, novice critiques were rated as valuable as expert critiques
Designers found feedback most useful when specific and emotionally positive; rubrics increased those traits
Expertise mainly increased length; experts may add value through clearer justification
practical_applications: Give any critic (human friend, AI) a rubric; ask for justification per point
limitations: Perceived value, not measured improvement; student designers; search-level reading

title: Parallel Prototyping Leads to Better Design Results, More Divergence, and Increased Self-Efficacy
authors: Steven P. Dow, Alana Glassco, Jonathan Kass, Melissa Schwarz, Daniel L. Schwartz, Scott R. Klemmer
key_findings: 33 participants designing web ads: making several prototypes before feedback (parallel) beat serial critique-after-each on click-through and expert ratings
Parallel produced more diverse designs and a gain in self-efficacy; serial did not
practical_applications: Critique 2-3 variants side by side rather than one image at a time
limitations: Small sample; replicated in engineering design by Murphy et al. 2022 (secondary)

title: The IKEA effect: When labor leads to love
authors: Michael I. Norton, Daniel Mochon, Dan Ariely
key_findings: Four studies (IKEA boxes, origami, Lego): people value what they built themselves more
Participants valued their amateur creations similarly to experts' and expected others to agree
Effect requires successful completion; destroyed or unfinished builds lost it
practical_applications: The maker (human or AI pipeline) overrates finished work it laboured on; route final judgement to someone who did not build it
limitations: Simple craft objects; one author (Ariely) has other papers under data-integrity scrutiny — this paper's findings have not been retracted as far as found; independent replications not checked here

title: Balancing on the Creative Highwire: Forecasting the Success of Novel Ideas in Organizations
authors: Justin M. Berg
key_findings: 339 circus professionals forecast audience success of new acts, checked against 13,248 audience members
Creators forecast peers' novel ideas more accurately than managers, but overestimated their own
Managers undervalued novel acts; best judges were peers who generate ideas but did not make the one judged; lab study: creator mindset improved ranking of novel ideas
practical_applications: Use peer creators (another agent/person who also makes work) as critics; never the author alone
limitations: Circus domain; read via Stanford GSB summary, not the ASQ paper

title: Discernment and creativity: How well can people identify their most creative ideas?
authors: Paul J. Silvia
key_findings: Cited as showing people were fairly discerning when picking their own most creative divergent-thinking responses (supports 'top-2' scoring)
Later literature argues evidence overall shows sub-optimal idea selection
practical_applications: Self-selection of best ideas is usable as a first filter, not a final verdict
limitations: Read only via citing papers; divergent-thinking tasks, not finished works

title: The Dunning-Kruger effect is (mostly) a statistical artefact: Valid approaches to testing the hypothesis with individual differences data
authors: Gilles E. Gignac, Marcin Zajenkowski
key_findings: IQ data from 929 people: classic DK pattern better explained by general overconfidence plus regression/measurement error
Challenged: Dunkel et al. 2023 found a significant but smaller DK effect in a representative sample; a 2023 comment questioned a recoding choice
practical_applications: Do not use 'Dunning-Kruger' to dismiss a maker's self-view; use external checks instead
limitations: Contested; read via abstracts/summaries

title: Reevaluating the Dunning-Kruger effect: A response to and replication of Gignac and Zajenkowski (2020)
authors: Curtis S. Dunkel, Joseph Nedelec, Dimitri van der Linden
key_findings: In a large nationally representative dataset a statistically significant DK effect appeared once sample and methods were addressed, but smaller in magnitude
practical_applications: Treat DK as small and contested; the robust lesson is general overconfidence in self-assessment
limitations: Search-snippet level

title: The Bias Blind Spot: Perceptions of Bias in Self Versus Others
authors: Emily Pronin, Daniel Y. Lin, Lee Ross
key_findings: People see biases much more in others than in themselves
Later accounts attribute it to introspection illusion, naive realism, self-enhancement; a pre-registered replication exists (Cambridge reader), status partly unclear
practical_applications: An AI or human critic saying 'I checked for bias' is not evidence; use procedural controls (blind, swap, rubric)
limitations: Search-level reading

title: A constant error in psychological ratings
authors: Edward L. Thorndike
key_findings: Officers' ratings of subordinates' separate traits (intelligence, physique, leadership, character) correlated too highly — a general good/bad impression coloured specific ratings; named the 'halo' error
practical_applications: Score criteria separately and before the overall verdict; do not let one striking strength set all scores
limitations: Historic; correlational

title: The halo effect: Evidence for unconscious alteration of judgments
authors: Richard E. Nisbett, Timothy D. Wilson
key_findings: A lecturer shown as warm vs cold was rated differently on appearance, mannerisms and accent (identical across conditions)
Participants were unaware of the influence and reported the reverse direction
practical_applications: A critic who likes the concept will rate execution higher — check execution items blind to concept
limitations: Single small experiment; search-level reading

title: Save the last dance for me: unwanted serial position effects in jury evaluations
authors: Wändi Bruine de Bruin
key_findings: Eurovision ratings rose with later performance position under both end-of-sequence and step-by-step scoring; same linear pattern in figure-skating step-by-step scores
Randomising order does not remove the effect but makes it fair
practical_applications: Randomise and rotate the order in which variants are shown to any critic; record order
limitations: Field data; mechanism proposed, not proven

title: Orchestrating Impartiality: The Impact of 'Blind' Auditions on Female Musicians
authors: Claudia Goldin, Cecilia Rouse
key_findings: Screen raised women's chance of advancing from preliminary rounds by ~50% and of winning finals several-fold; explains 30-55% of the rise in female new hires
Critique (Gelman 2019 as reported in press): estimates noisy, many not statistically significant; a 2017 Australian public-service trial found de-identification reduced women's shortlisting
practical_applications: Blind review removes identity cues, but its effect depends on context — test, don't assume
limitations: Contested precision; abstract-level reading

title: A reliability-generalization study of journal peer reviews: a multilevel meta-analysis of inter-rater reliability and its determinants
authors: Lutz Bornmann, Rüdiger Mutz, Hans-Dieter Daniel
key_findings: 70 coefficients from 48 studies, 19,443 manuscripts: inter-rater reliability of journal peer review is low (mean ICC/r2 = .34, kappa = .17)
Larger studies report lower IRR; studies reporting high IRR are less credible
practical_applications: Even expert reviewers often disagree; one critic's verdict is a sample, not the truth — aggregate several
limitations: Scientific manuscripts, not creative works

title: Social psychology of creativity: A consensual assessment technique
authors: Teresa M. Amabile
key_findings: (via Cseh & Jeffries) independent expert judges rating relative to the sample reach acceptable agreement; collage study: psychologists .73, art teachers .88
practical_applications: Use several independent judges who rate without discussion, items in different random orders
limitations: Not read directly

title: A scattered CAT: A critical evaluation of the Consensual Assessment Technique for creativity research
authors: Genevieve M. Cseh, Karl K. Jeffries
key_findings: CAT guidelines: judges with domain experience, rate independently without training or discussion, rate relative to the sample, see items in different random orders, rate other dimensions (technical, aesthetic) separately
Expert vs novice agreement is equivocal and domain-dependent; adding judges (>10) can inflate alpha; <5 judges risks both error types
Reporting of CAT procedures is inconsistent; calls for harmonised protocol
practical_applications: Studio panel: 3-5 independent raters (human + different AI models) rating relatively, before any discussion
limitations: Review of research use, not of studio practice

title: A Structured Approach to Strategic Decisions
authors: Daniel Kahneman, Dan Lovallo, Olivier Sibony
key_findings: Mediating Assessments Protocol: define a few attributes in advance, assess each independently on facts, delay the holistic judgement to the end ('delay intuition')
Authors admit effectiveness is hard to quantify; reduces but does not remove variability
practical_applications: Critic fills each criterion before the total; total written last
limitations: Read via summaries; management decisions

title: Liz Lerman's Critical Response Process (official page); book: Critique Is Creative (Lerman & Borstel)
authors: Liz Lerman; John Borstel
key_findings: Devised 1990; four steps: Statements of Meaning; Artist as Questioner; Neutral Questions ('do not have an opinion couched in them'); Permissioned Opinions (artist may say no)
Roles: artist/maker, responders (committed to the artist's intent to make excellent work), facilitator
practical_applications: Start a critique with what works and what it means; ask neutral questions before opinions
limitations: Practitioner method; no controlled outcome studies found

title: Creativity, Inc. (Braintrust chapter) / How Pixar Fosters Collective Creativity (HBR 2008)
authors: Ed Catmull, Amy Wallace
key_findings: (via summaries) Braintrust gives candid notes to a director but has no authority; the director decides
HBR 2008 summary: creative authority placed with project leaders rather than executives
practical_applications: Separate critic (advises) from owner (decides); critic notes are inputs
limitations: Insider account; full text not accessible (403); secondary summaries only

title: Feldman's Model of Art Criticism (teaching handout)
authors: Grand Valley State University (after Edmund Burke Feldman)
key_findings: Description (obvious visual qualities), Analysis (formal elements and principles), Interpretation (meaning proposed from evidence), Judgment (merit; 'usually used with mature audiences')
practical_applications: Template for AI critique order: describe -> analyse -> interpret -> judge
limitations: Handout, not Feldman's own text

title: Art as Image and Idea / Varieties of Visual Experience
authors: Edmund Burke Feldman
key_findings: (via secondary) interpretation is the central and most important part of criticism; formal analysis accumulates evidence for interpretation and judgement
practical_applications: Analysis serves interpretation; do not stop at a list of formal faults
limitations: Edition/date details conflict across sources; not read

title: Criticizing Art: Understanding the Contemporary
authors: Terry Barrett
key_findings: (via summaries/handouts) artworks are about something and call for interpretation; interpretations are persuasive arguments; some are better than others, judged by coherence, correspondence, inclusiveness
A work is not necessarily about what the artist intended; interpret in the work's best light; interpretation is individual and communal
practical_applications: Critic must argue from visible evidence and account for all of it (inclusiveness)
limitations: Read via handout summaries only

title: Review of Noël Carroll, On Criticism (Routledge 2009)
authors: Alan H. Goldman
key_findings: Carroll: criticism aims essentially at reasoned evaluation; description, classification, analysis, interpretation supply the reasons
Carroll's success-value: did the artist succeed in the aims intended (intentionalism); forgery argument
Goldman's objections: anti-intentionalist constraints, works as public objects, value from historical impact, local principles are genre-relative
practical_applications: For commissioned work, judge success against the stated brief (intent is documented), but allow value beyond intent
limitations: Review of the book, not the book itself

title: Art criticism (Encyclopaedia Britannica entry)
authors: Encyclopaedia Britannica
key_findings: Vasari's Lives (1550) seminal early criticism; Diderot reviewed the Paris Salons 1759-1781; Baudelaire's Salons (1845, 1846); Ruskin defended Turner in Modern Painters (1843); Greenberg 'Avant-Garde and Kitsch' (1939)
Best surveys: Venturi History of Art Criticism (1936), Schlosser Die Kunstliteratur (1924)
practical_applications: Historical context for the critic role
limitations: Page blocked (403); facts via search snippets

title: Cours de peinture par principes (Balance des peintres)
authors: Roger de Piles
key_findings: Scored ~56-57 painters 0-20 on composition, drawing, colour, expression; discussed by 18th-c critics, ridiculed by Hogarth
practical_applications: Earliest famous multi-criterion art score — and an early example of a rubric reflecting the rater's school (colourist) bias
limitations: Via Wikipedia/secondary; painter count differs between sources

title: A Foucauldian look at the design jury
authors: Helena Webster
key_findings: Year-long ethnography in a British architecture school: juries heightened judgement and produced unintended learning outcomes
Critics brought personal paradigms; non-conforming students castigated with harsh epithets; most exchanges were monologues; students often did not understand critics' language
Students responded strategically ('draw up the tutor's sketches'), reducing risk-taking; only students aligned to the paradigm experienced real dialogue
practical_applications: Critique against the brief, in plain language, as dialogue; harsh verdicts make makers play safe
limitations: Single school ethnography; author notes no generalisability

title: Design Juries on Trial: The Renaissance of the Design Studio
authors: Kathryn H. Anthony
key_findings: Research with 900+ people over 7 years (observation, videos, student diaries, surveys); fuelled the AIAS Studio Culture Task Force report (2002)
practical_applications: Background on reform of the studio crit
limitations: Findings not read directly

title: Iowa Writers' Workshop — Our History
authors: University of Iowa
key_findings: Founded 1936 (Wilbur Schramm); prototype for 300+ writing programmes; weekly peer critique of new work
practical_applications: Origin of the 'workshop' critique format
limitations: Institutional page via search; 'silent author' rule not documented in sources found

title: Hierarchy, 'Kreng Jai' and Feedback: A Grounded Theory Study Exploring Perspectives of Clinical Faculty and Medical Students in Thailand
authors: Rosawan S. Areemit, Cooper CM, Wirasorn K, Paopongsawan P, Panthongviriyakul C, Subha Ramani
key_findings: Thai hierarchy perpetuates top-down feedback; kreng jai affects feedback seeking and giving
Students accept harsh feedback when it includes suggestions for improvement; feedback most credible when the giver knows the effort
'One size feedback training does not fit all'
practical_applications: Thai collaborators may not volunteer criticism to the owner/user — ask specific neutral questions; always pair a problem with a fix
limitations: Medical education, one centre, qualitative
